# Abstract

**Background**  
STEPS measures biological NCD burden; DHS captures self-reported diagnosis and insurance. We estimated Kenya STEPS 2015 care cascades, compared them with KDHS 2022 self-report, and validated a dual-survey estimator of population unmet need before the Social Health Authority (SHA) transition.

**Methods**  
Design-based analysis of STEPS 2015 (n=4,500; ages 18–69) for measured hypertension (BP ≥140/90 mmHg or on medication) and diabetes (fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L or on medication), with awareness, treatment, and control among those with disease. KDHS 2022 adults (n=40,636; women ≤49, men ≤54) provided self-reported diagnosis, treatment among the diagnosed, and insurance (PR `sh27`). A detection ratio and hybrid estimator (STEPS awareness × DHS treatment|diagnosed) were compared with STEPS-direct treatment. STROBE reporting.

**Results**  
Measured hypertension prevalence was 24.2% (95% CI 21.8–26.7) and diabetes 2.0% (1.3–2.6). Among hypertensives, 23.7% (19.7–27.7) were aware, 7.8% (5.7–9.8) treated, and 2.7% (0.9–4.5) controlled. Men were less aware (16.0% vs 31.8%) and treated (3.8% vs 11.8%) than women. Only 0.6% of all adults had controlled hypertension. KDHS self-reported hypertension was 4.4% (4.1–4.7; detection ratio 0.18); 34.0% (30.4–37.5) of diagnosed adults were treated and 48.1% (44.7–51.4) insured. Hybrid treatment among measured hypertension was 8.0%, matching STEPS-direct 7.8%.

**Conclusions**  
Most hypertension was undiagnosed or uncontrolled. DHS self-report sees a minority of measured disease; treatment gaps among the diagnosed describe a visible subset only. SHA monitoring should track detection and control, not enrolment alone.

**Keywords:** hypertension; diabetes; care cascade; underdiagnosis; STEPS; Demographic and Health Survey; Kenya; Social Health Authority


# Background

Hypertension and diabetes drive a growing share of premature death and disability in sub-Saharan Africa, yet health systems still detect and control only a minority of cases [@zhou2021global; @gesesew2020cascade; @manne2019diabetes; @atun2017diabetes]. Kenya's last nationally measured non-communicable disease (NCD) risk-factor survey—the 2015 WHO STEPwise survey—documented high blood pressure, low awareness, and incomplete treatment [@kenyaSTEPS2015; @mohamed2018prevalence; @mohamed2018diabetes; @wamai2014kenya]. The 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS) added self-reported NCD diagnosis and treatment items and, in the Person Recode, health insurance status on the eve of the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) transition to the Social Health Authority (SHA) in October 2024 [@kdhs2022; @sha2024kenya].

These two survey systems are complementary but rarely analysed jointly with an explicit measurement model. STEPS measures blood pressure and fasting glucose and therefore can construct a biological care cascade from disease to control [@whoSTEPS; @vardeny2019care]. DHS asks whether respondents were ever told they have a condition and whether they take medication, and can link diagnosis to insurance—but it does not measure blood pressure or glucose in the adult sample. Analyses restricted to self-reported diagnosis, including our related KDHS 2022 study of insurance and treatment gaps among diagnosed adults [@amollo2026st03], necessarily condition on the people who have already been detected by the health system. That conditioning can make population unmet need look smaller than it is.

Cross-country STEPS analyses show large leakages at every cascade step in low- and middle-income countries [@gesesew2020cascade; @manne2019diabetes]. Kenyan facility and household studies document cost barriers and incomplete coverage for chronic care [@amollo2026kisumu; @barasa2018extending; @kazungu2017examining]. What remains under-used is a transparent dual-survey design that: (i) re-estimates the measured cascade with equity stratification; (ii) quantifies how much of measured disease self-report surveys can see; and (iii) tests whether a simple transportability estimator—STEPS awareness times DHS treatment among the diagnosed—recovers the STEPS-measured treatment rate. If it does, the same framework can be used when only one survey type is available, and it reframes insurance-linked gaps among the diagnosed as the tip of a population iceberg.

We therefore had three objectives. First, to estimate survey-weighted measured hypertension and diabetes care cascades in Kenya STEPS 2015, including population-level treatment and control coverage and sex, residence, and education differences. Second, to estimate self-reported diagnosis prevalence, treatment among the diagnosed, and insurance among the diagnosed in KDHS 2022 for adults in the STEPS age window, insofar as DHS age ceilings allow. Third, to define and validate dual-survey estimators of detection and hybrid population treatment coverage, and to discuss implications for SHA-era monitoring.

# Methods

## Study design and reporting

We conducted a dual-survey secondary analysis of two nationally representative cross-sectional household surveys. The study is reported according to STROBE guidance for observational studies [@vonelm2007strobe]. No individual-level record linkage was possible or attempted; synthesis is at the estimator level.

## Data sources

### Kenya STEPS 2015

STEPS 2015 used a three-step WHO instrument: interview (Step 1), physical measurements including blood pressure, height, and weight (Step 2), and biochemistry including fasting blood glucose and total cholesterol (Step 3) [@kenyaSTEPS2015; @whoSTEPS]. The public-use file contains 4,500 adults aged 18–69 years with design variables `psu`, `stratum`, and analysis weights `wstep1`, `wstep2`, and `wstep3` for the three steps.

### Kenya DHS 2022

We used the women's recode (IR; ages 15–49), men's recode (MR; ages 15–54), and Person Recode (PR) for insurance (`sh27`, `sh28a`). Adults were restricted to ages 18–69 to approximate the STEPS range, noting that DHS still truncates women at 49 and men at 54 years. Insurance was merged on cluster, household, and line number (`hv001`/`v001`, `hv002`/`v002`, `hvidx`/`v003`), following the KDHS 2022 architecture in which standard individual insurance fields are empty and coverage is carried in PR [@kdhs2022; @amollo2026st03]. Men's weights were adjusted by a strata-specific male subsample factor derived from PR eligibility, as in our prior pooled analyses [@amollo2026st03].

## Outcome definitions

### STEPS measured disease and cascade

Systolic and diastolic blood pressure were the averages of the second and third readings. **Measured hypertension** was systolic pressure ≥140 mmHg, diastolic pressure ≥90 mmHg, or current blood-pressure medication. **Measured diabetes** was fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L or current glucose-lowering medication. Among people with measured disease:

- **Aware:** ever told of raised blood pressure (or glucose) by a health worker, or currently on medication  
- **Treated:** currently on medication  
- **Controlled:** on medication and below clinical thresholds (blood pressure <140/90 mmHg; glucose <7.0 mmol/L)

**Population treatment coverage** was prevalence × treatment among those with disease; **population control coverage** was prevalence × control among those with disease. Body-mass index used measured height and weight; overweight or obesity was BMI ≥25 kg/m² and obesity BMI ≥30 kg/m².

### DHS self-report

**Diagnosed hypertension** and **diagnosed diabetes** were self-report of ever being told by a health professional (KDHS NCD module). **Treated among diagnosed** was current medication among those who reported a diagnosis. **Any insurance** was PR `sh27`.

### Dual-survey estimators

We defined a **detection ratio** DR = p̂_dx,DHS / p̂_measured,STEPS and an **underdiagnosis index** UDI = max(0, 1 − DR). These quantities compare measurement systems and calendar years; they are not time-trend estimators and are not interpreted as change from 2015 to 2022.

We defined a **hybrid treated-among-measured** estimator under a transportability assumption: τ̂_hybrid = â_STEPS × t̂_DHS, where â_STEPS is awareness among measured disease and t̂_DHS is treatment among self-reported diagnosed disease. Population hybrid treatment coverage is p̂_measured × τ̂_hybrid. We compared τ̂_hybrid with STEPS-direct treatment among measured disease. Sensitivity analyses multiplied â and t̂ by 0.8 and 1.2 (capped at 1).

## Statistical analysis

All prevalence and cascade estimates used sampling weights with design-based standard errors from the ultimate-cluster (linearised) variance estimator, treating primary sampling units as clusters and survey strata as strata [@lumley2004]. STEPS analyses used the weight matching the measurement step (`wstep2` for blood pressure and anthropometry; `wstep3` for glucose and cholesterol). DHS analyses used individual weights with the male subsample correction. We report percentages with 95% confidence intervals and unweighted denominators.

Socioeconomic patterning of STEPS hypertension outcomes used education as an ordinal rank (no formal schooling through postgraduate) and the Erreygers-corrected concentration index for binary outcomes, with percentile intervals from a 200-replicate cluster bootstrap [@erreygers2009; @odonnell2008]. Stratified cascade estimates were produced by sex, urban–rural residence, and collapsed education groups.

Analyses were implemented in Python 3 with design-based estimators; scripts and table outputs are archived with the study package. Item non-response was handled by domain restriction with complete cases for each estimator. We make no causal claims.

## Ethical considerations

STEPS and KDHS are de-identified public-use datasets collected under national ethical approvals. This secondary analysis used DHS data under authorisation reference 220623 (granted 20 October 2025) and STEPS microdata under authorised research access. No additional participant contact occurred.

# Results

## STEPS sample and risk-factor context

Among 4,500 STEPS participants, design-weighted composition was approximately half women (51.1%) and about three-fifths urban (62.1%). Primary education was the modal group (45.6%). Weighted overweight or obesity was 27.6 (24.5–30.7)% and obesity 9.0 (7.5–10.4)%. Only 44.2 (40.2–48.1)% of adults reported ever having had blood pressure measured, and 11.9 (9.5–14.3)% ever having had blood glucose measured.

## Measured hypertension cascade

Measured hypertension affected 24.2 (21.8–26.7)% of adults (unweighted n with Step 2 measures = 4441). Among 1,227 adults with measured hypertension, awareness was 23.7 (19.7–27.7)%, medication use 7.8 (5.7–9.8)%, and control 2.7 (0.9–4.5)% (Table 1; Figure 1). Among the minority on treatment, control was 34.4 (16.4–52.5)%. Thus more than three-quarters of people with hypertension did not know their status, more than nine in ten were not on medication, and about 97.3% remained uncontrolled.

At population level, antihypertensive medication covered only 1.9% of all adults, and controlled hypertension only 0.6% (Figure 4). The population fraction with uncontrolled measured hypertension was 23.6%—almost equal to the prevalence itself, because control was rare.

Sex differences were large (Figure 2). Hypertension prevalence was similar in men (25.3 (22.0–28.6)%) and women (23.2 (20.6–25.9)%), but awareness among those with disease was 16.0 (10.6–21.3)% in men versus 31.8 (26.9–36.6)% in women, and treatment 3.8 (1.9–5.8)% versus 11.8 (7.8–15.9)%. Control among men with hypertension was about 1%.

Education-related inequality in prevalence and cascade stages was modest: Erreygers indices were close to zero with bootstrap intervals spanning zero for prevalence, treatment, and control (Table 2). Absolute cascade failure was therefore a population-wide problem rather than a narrow pro-rich or pro-poor pattern by education.

## Measured diabetes cascade

Measured diabetes prevalence was 2.0 (1.3–2.6)% (n = 4178 in the Step 3 domain). Among people with measured diabetes (n = 117), awareness was 28.0 (13.6–42.4)%, treatment 22.7 (9.1–36.2)%, and control 6.6 (2.0–11.3)% (Table 1; Figure 1). Confidence intervals were wide because the diabetes numerator was small, but the qualitative pattern matched hypertension: most disease was not controlled. Combined measured hypertension or diabetes affected about one-quarter of adults with both measurements available.

## KDHS 2022 self-report, treatment, and insurance

In KDHS 2022 adults in the restricted age window (n = 40,636), self-reported hypertension diagnosis was 4.4 (4.1–4.7)% and diabetes diagnosis 0.8 (0.7–0.9)% (Table 3). Among those with diagnosed hypertension, 34.0 (30.4–37.5)% reported current medication (treatment gap about 66.0%). Among those with diagnosed diabetes, medication use was higher (70.2 (62.6–77.7)%). Any health insurance covered 48.1 (44.7–51.4)% of adults with diagnosed hypertension and 47.7 (44.4–50.9)% of adults with either diagnosis—figures aligned with our prior diagnosed-adult analysis [@amollo2026st03]. Treatment among diagnosed hypertension was higher in the insured (39.7% [33.6–45.9]) than the uninsured (28.4% [24.7–32.1]), but even insured diagnosed adults fell far short of universal treatment.

## Dual-survey synthesis

The hypertension detection ratio (DHS self-report over STEPS measured prevalence) was **0.18**, corresponding to an underdiagnosis index of **82%** of measured disease not represented in self-report prevalence (Figure 3; Table 4). For diabetes the detection ratio was **0.41** (underdiagnosis index 59%). These ratios mix measurement modality, survey year, and age-structure differences and must not be read as a seven-year trend.

The hybrid estimator for hypertension—STEPS awareness × DHS treatment among the diagnosed—yielded **8.0%** treated among measured disease, compared with the STEPS-direct estimate of **7.8 (5.7–9.8)%**. Agreement within one percentage point supports transportability of treatment-conditional-on-diagnosis from DHS to the STEPS awareness structure for hypertension. For diabetes, hybrid treatment among measured disease was 19.6% versus STEPS-direct 22.7 (9.1–36.2)%, with wider uncertainty.

Sensitivity analyses for hypertension (Table 5) kept population untreated disease between about 21% and 23% of adults across ±20% relative shifts in awareness and treatment-among-diagnosed, because prevalence is high and both cascade steps are low. Conclusions about large population unmet need are robust to moderate misspecification of the hybrid components.

# Discussion

## Principal findings

Three findings structure the dual-survey picture. First, measured hypertension was common in Kenya STEPS 2015 (24.2%), but control among those with disease was rare (2.7%), so nearly a quarter of all adults carried uncontrolled hypertension. Second, men and women had similar measured prevalence, yet men were systematically less aware and less treated—an engagement gap that pure prevalence studies understate. Third, KDHS 2022 self-report prevalence was several-fold lower than STEPS-measured prevalence, while treatment among the diagnosed remained incomplete and only partly aligned with insurance. A hybrid estimator linking STEPS awareness to DHS treatment recovered the STEPS-measured treatment rate for hypertension, validating a practical dual-survey identity: **population treatment ≈ measured prevalence × awareness × treatment among the diagnosed**.

## Relation to prior work

Our measured hypertension prevalence (24.2%) is close to the published STEPS-based national estimate of about 24.5% [@mohamed2018prevalence], supporting definitional fidelity. We intentionally move beyond prevalence replication to cascade control, sex-specific leakage, population-level coverage, and dual-survey methods. Global multi-country cascades report similarly severe drop-offs from disease to control in low-resource settings [@gesesew2020cascade; @manne2019diabetes; @jorgensen2020zanzibar]. Our related KDHS analysis showed that among diagnosed adults, insurance coverage was incomplete and treatment gaps exceeded 60% for combined hypertension or diabetes [@amollo2026st03]. The present study shows why that finding, while policy-relevant for people already labelled with disease, understates population unmet need: most people with measured hypertension never enter the diagnosed denominator.

## Methods contribution

The dual-survey framework formalises what analysts often do informally. Detection ratios quantify how much biological burden self-report surveys miss. Hybrid estimators allow DHS-based health-financing variables—insurance, payment barriers—to be discussed against a STEPS-informed disease base when simultaneous measurement of insurance and biomarkers is unavailable. Validation against STEPS-direct treatment is essential; without it, hybrid products can hide incompatible definitions. We recommend that future Kenyan NCD monitoring either (i) restore periodic STEPS-like measurement with insurance and care modules in the same questionnaire, or (ii) publish dual-survey dashboards that report diagnosed-adult indicators and population cascade indicators side by side under explicit assumptions.

## Policy implications for the SHA era

SHA reforms that expand enrolment without measuring detection and control will appear successful on administrative dashboards while population blood-pressure control remains near zero. Our population control coverage of about 0.6% of adults is a stark pre-SHA biological baseline. Priority implications include: opportunistic and community blood-pressure screening that reaches men; reliable antihypertensive supply and adherence support after diagnosis; and SHA benefit design that links membership to chronic-care continuity, not only acute visit coverage [@amollo2026kisumu; @barasa2018extending]. Diabetes absolute numbers are smaller but control remains poor among those with disease, and self-report still under-captures measured hyperglycaemia.

## Strengths and limitations

Strengths include nationally representative microdata for both surveys, design-based variance estimation, pre-specified cascade definitions aligned with WHO STEPS practice, equity indices, and a hybrid estimator validated against measured treatment. Limitations are substantial and must frame interpretation. STEPS and DHS are seven years apart; detection ratios are structural comparisons, not trends. DHS age ceilings exclude older women and men who carry high NCD burden, which likely **inflates** underdiagnosis indices relative to a true 18–69 self-report census. Self-report and measured disease use different constructs; medication questions and skip patterns are not identical across surveys. STEPS lacks insurance variables, so insurance findings remain DHS-only. Diabetes numerators in STEPS are small, widening intervals. Education is an imperfect SES proxy compared with DHS wealth quintiles. Cross-sectional design precludes causal claims about insurance or sex.

# Conclusions

In Kenya STEPS 2015, about one in four adults had measured hypertension, yet only about one in forty people with hypertension had controlled blood pressure, and only about 0.6% of all adults were controlled. KDHS 2022 self-report saw a fraction of that burden, and even among the diagnosed, treatment and insurance were incomplete. A dual-survey hybrid estimator recovered STEPS-measured treatment rates for hypertension and shows how financing analyses among the diagnosed can be rescaled to population unmet need. As Kenya implements SHA, monitoring should track not only enrolment but detection, treatment, and control—especially for men and for people who never appear in self-report denominators.

DHS data were accessed under project authorisation reference 220623 (20 October 2025). No new consent was required.

Analysis scripts and derived non-identifiable summary tables for this study are available in the study package; raw microdata are not redistributed.
